sealed_thresholds.note: registered BEFORE measurement; never tuned to results (Art. XXVII)
sealed_thresholds.ensemble: NONE (single-attacker calibration only; majority-vote ensembles are deferred by the R412 directive)

escalation.reason: measured FPR 1.0 > sealed bar 0.3 (Art. L: the attacker is measured non-selective; its KILL is inadmissible as a terminal verdict and is escalated with the objection preserved)
escalation.rule: the instrument's KILL is measured non-selective (FPR above the sealed bar); the objection is preserved verbatim and ESCALATED for adjudication — the candidate is NOT killed by this attack alone (Art. L); the deterministic gates are unchanged

preserved_objections.basis: The proposed mechanism assumes free chlorine selective pressure directly controls biofilm characteristics, but evidence [doi:10.1038/s41522-020-00144-w] shows that residual chlorine impacts are highly complex and non-linear, with unpredictable effects on different microbial communities, making the claimed selective pressure relationship oversimplified and unreliable.

Evidence [doi:10.1038/s41522-023-00473-6] directly contradicts the prediction by showing that elevated water age (which would occur in summer demand conditions) leads to increased nitrite accumulation regardless of chlorine concentration, suggesting the proposed intervention cannot overcome this fundamental hydraulic limitation.

The candidate cannot beat the baseline because maintaining total chlorine residual above 1.0 mg/L while reducing free chlorine concentration is chemically impossible in chloraminated systems where free chlorine and combined chlorine exist in equilibrium, as shown in evidence [doi:10.1007/s11274-026-05101-x].

The proposed "optimal free chlorine concentration threshold" cannot be implemented because chlorine distribution in water mains follows complex hydraulic patterns with significant spatial and temporal variation, making uniform concentration control impossible as evidenced by [doi:10.1016/j.mex.2018.06.015].
